newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB sees 1997/98 world coarse grains prices lower.
newsitem.headline: CWB sees 1997/98 world coarse grains prices lower.

text.p: Prices of world coarse grains are expected to fall by five to 10 percent in the 1997/98 (Oct/Sept) season from the prior year as stockpiles increase, Canadian Wheat Board (CWB) market analyst Fred Oleson said.

Oleson, addressing the CWB's annual Grain World meeting, said 1997/98 world production of coarse grains -- corn, barley, oats, sorghum, rye, millet and mixed grains -- would fall three million tonnes to 885 million, with consumption up 9 million tonnes to 880 million.

But 1995/96 production of 888 million tonnes was up 90 million tonnes, boosting beginning and end-season world stocks and providing enough supply to offset more demand from Asia, North Africa and Latin America.
World end-stocks of coarse grains would rise to 114.2 million tonnes in 1997/98 from 109.2 million in 1996/97 and 92.2 million in 1995/96. Stocks totalled 134.9 million at the end of 1994/95.
"Higher production in the U.S. is offset by lower production in the European Union, China and Canada," Oleson said of the coarse grains to be harvested starting this fall.

He said U.S. corn production should rise about 7 million tonnes to 243 million (or 9.5 billion bushels) due to larger plantings. Seeding of 81 million acres was expected with a shift back to corn from 1.5 million acres planted to soybeans last year due to wet conditions.
Some soft red winter wheat areas may also shift to corn, Oleson said. The farm price of U.S. corn in 1997/98 should average $2.50 a bushel, down from $2.70 in 1995/96, he said.

Although U.S. corn exports and feed use in 1997/98 were expected to rise, end-stocks were still projected at 1.25 billion bushels, up from 969 million in August 1997. But U.S. stocks will still be at historically low levels, Oleson said.

Oleson said the world stocks-to-use ratio for coarse grains at the end of 1997/98 was expected to rise only to 13.0 percent, up from 12.5 percent in the current year and the record low ratio of 11.0 percent at the end of 1995/96.

Due to falling corn yields, China is expected to be a net importer of corn in 1997/98 after briefly becoming a net exporter of corn last year, Oleson said. From 1992 to 1997, Chinese corn consumption rose by an average 7 million tonnes annually.
Oleson said currently China's 1997/98 corn imports were seen at 1.5 million tonnes and exports at 500,000 tonnes.
"Imports could be significantly higher if total consumption increases at the rate at which it has increased, on average, over the last five years," Oleson said.
Canadian corn production would rise slightly at 7.3 million tonnes but from 7.239 million but total coarse grains output fall to 25 million tonnes from 28.4 million in 1996/97.
Imports of U.S. corn into Western Canada and Ontario will rise in 1997/98 due to lower U.S. prices, Oleson said.
Oleson said exports of Canadian oats to the U.S. in 1996/97 should total 1.25 million tonnes and be similar in 1997/98, with subsidized exports from Sweden and Finland the main competition.
Canadian oats production in 1997/98 would fall to 3.075 million tonnes from 4.374 million in 1996/97, with expected plantings at 1.593 million hectares against 2.058 million.
Oleson said factors to watch this spring for coarse grains included potential flooding in Manitoba and North Dakota and other weather conditions in the U.S., Europe and China.
"Given that carry-in stocks are tight, any serious production problems could cause significantly higher prices," Oleson said.
